notes.definition: Biotic factors are the living factors in an environment, such as the availability of food, predators, pathogens and competition from other species, that affect the organisms in a community.
explanation: Biotic factors are the effects that living organisms have on each other. AQA lists four biotic factors that can affect a community: the availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; and one species outcompeting another so that the numbers of the losing species are no longer sufficient to breed. You need to be able to explain how a change in any of these could affect a community, using data or information you are given.

Availability of food affects how many animals can survive and reproduce. When food is plentiful, more individuals survive and breed, so the population grows. When food is scarce, competition for it increases, some animals starve or fail to breed, and the population falls. Food availability itself often depends on other factors, for example a cold spring may delay plant growth, so there is less food for herbivores.

New predators arriving in an area can cause a big fall in the numbers of their prey, especially if the prey have never met that predator before and have no way of avoiding it. For example, when rats and cats were introduced to remote islands, many ground-nesting birds that had evolved without predators were wiped out. The effect then spreads to other species in the food web, because the prey species were food for other animals or ate plants themselves.

New pathogens (disease-causing microorganisms) can spread quickly through a population that has no resistance. Ash dieback, a fungal disease, is killing large numbers of ash trees in Britain. Myxomatosis, a virus, killed most of Britain's rabbits in the 1950s, which changed grassland plants and reduced numbers of rabbit predators. Because the infected species is interdependent with others, a new disease affects the whole community.

When two species compete for the same resources, one may be better at obtaining them. If one species outcompetes another, the losing species gets too little food, light or space. Its numbers may fall so low that there are no longer enough individuals to find mates and breed, and it may disappear from the area. The red squirrel has been outcompeted by the introduced grey squirrel in most of England.

In a stable community the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles. If prey numbers rise, there is more food for predators, so predator numbers rise a little later. More predators eat more prey, so prey numbers fall, and then predator numbers fall too because there is less food. This is an example of how food availability (a biotic factor) controls population size.
keyFacts: Biotic factors are living factors that affect a community.
AQA biotic factors: availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another.
More food means more animals survive and reproduce, so the population increases.
New predators can sharply reduce prey populations, especially prey with no defences against them.
New pathogens can spread rapidly in a population with no resistance (for example ash dieback, myxomatosis).
If one species outcompetes another, the losing species' numbers may fall too low to breed.
Changes to one species spread through the community because of interdependence.
Predator and prey numbers rise and fall in cycles, with predator peaks after prey peaks.

keyTerms.definition: A living factor that affects organisms in a community, such as food availability, predators, pathogens or competitors.
An animal that kills and eats other animals.
An animal that is killed and eaten by a predator.
A microorganism that causes infectious disease, such as a virus, bacterium, fungus or protist.
To be more successful than another species at obtaining the same limited resources.
A species brought into an area (often by humans) where it did not live before.
The repeated rise and fall of predator and prey populations, with the predator population lagging behind the prey population.

workedExamples.title: Explaining the effect of a new pathogen
workedExamples.question: In the 1950s the virus that causes myxomatosis killed about 99% of rabbits in Britain. Explain how this affected grassland plants and foxes.
steps: The virus is a new pathogen: a biotic factor.
With very few rabbits, much less grass was eaten.
Grass grew taller and shrubs and trees began to grow, shading out small flowering plants that need light.
Rabbits were food for foxes, so foxes had less food; fewer survived and bred, so fox numbers fell (some switched to other prey).
workedExamples.answer: Less grazing let grass, shrubs and trees grow taller, shading out short plants; foxes lost a major food source so their numbers fell.

workedExamples.title: Reading a predator-prey cycle
workedExamples.question: On a graph of lynx and snowshoe hare numbers, hares peak at 140 thousand in year 4 and lynx peak at 8 thousand in year 5. Explain why the lynx peak comes after the hare peak.
steps: As hare numbers rise, more food is available, so more lynx survive and breed.
It takes time for lynx to reproduce and for young to grow, so their numbers rise a year later.
Lynx then eat so many hares that hare numbers fall.
workedExamples.answer: Predator numbers depend on prey (food) availability; there is a delay while predators breed, so the predator peak lags about one year behind the prey peak.

workedExamples.title: Percentage fall after a new predator
workedExamples.question: An island had 2500 nesting seabirds. Two years after rats arrived there were 600. Calculate the percentage decrease.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often list temperature or light as biotic factors.
misconceptions.right: In fact these are abiotic (non-living). Biotic factors involve living organisms: food, predators, pathogens and competitors.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think predator and prey numbers peak at the same time.
misconceptions.right: In fact the predator peak comes after the prey peak, because predators need time to breed after their food supply increases.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a species only disappears when every individual is killed.
misconceptions.right: In fact a population can fail once numbers are too low to find mates and breed, even if some individuals are still alive.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a new predator only affects its prey.
misconceptions.right: In fact the effect spreads: the prey's food may increase, and other predators of that prey lose food.

realWorld: Ash dieback, a fungal pathogen, is expected to kill most ash trees in the UK, affecting insects, lichens and birds that depend on ash.
Introduced American mink have caused a large fall in UK water vole numbers because water voles have no defence against this new predator.
Conservation groups protect red squirrels by controlling grey squirrel numbers in areas such as Anglesey and northern Scotland.
examTips: Learn the four AQA biotic factors: food availability, new predators, new pathogens, and one species outcompeting another.
For 'explain the effect of' questions, give a chain of at least two or three linked steps, for example: fewer prey, less food for predators, fewer predators survive and breed.
On predator-prey graphs, describe the lag: the predator peak comes after the prey peak. Use numbers and years from the graph.
If asked why a species disappeared even though not all individuals were killed, say numbers became too low to breed successfully.
summary: Biotic factors are living factors that affect communities.
Food availability controls how many animals can survive and breed.
New predators and new pathogens can cause sharp falls in populations with no defences or resistance.
A species outcompeted by another may fall below the numbers needed to breed.
Changes spread through the community because species are interdependent.
Predator and prey populations rise and fall in cycles, with the predator lagging behind.

flashcards.back: A living factor that affects organisms in a community.

flashcards.front: List the four biotic factors named by AQA.
flashcards.back: Availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another so numbers are too low to breed.

flashcards.front: Why can a new predator wipe out a prey species?
flashcards.back: The prey has not evolved defences against it, so many are eaten and numbers fall rapidly.

flashcards.front: Give an example of a new pathogen affecting a UK community.
flashcards.back: Ash dieback (fungus) killing ash trees, or myxomatosis (virus) killing rabbits.

flashcards.front: What happens to a population when food becomes scarce?
flashcards.back: Competition increases; fewer survive and reproduce, so the population falls.

flashcards.front: Why might a species disappear even if not all individuals die?
flashcards.back: Numbers become too low to find mates and breed.

flashcards.front: Give an example of one species outcompeting another.
flashcards.back: Grey squirrels outcompeting red squirrels for food in Britain.

flashcards.front: In a predator-prey cycle, which population peaks first?
Why does the predator peak lag behind the prey peak?
flashcards.back: Predators need time to reproduce after their food supply increases.

flashcards.front: Why do prey numbers fall after predator numbers rise?
Is a disease-causing bacterium a biotic or abiotic factor?
Give one effect of rabbits dying out on grassland plants.
flashcards.back: Grass grows taller and shades out small flowering plants; shrubs and trees may start to grow.

questions.question: Which of these is a biotic factor?
options: Temperature
Availability of food
Soil pH
Wind direction
markScheme: 1 mark: availability of food
questions.explanation: Food comes from living organisms, so its availability is biotic. Temperature, soil pH and wind are non-living (abiotic).

questions.question: What is a pathogen?
options: An animal that eats other animals
A plant that makes its own food
A microorganism that causes disease
A species that competes for light
markScheme: 1 mark: a microorganism that causes disease
questions.explanation: Pathogens are disease-causing microorganisms such as viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists. An animal that eats other animals is a predator.

questions.question: Which list contains only biotic factors?
options: New predators, new pathogens, availability of food
Light intensity, new predators, temperature
Moisture, pathogens, carbon dioxide level
Soil pH, competition, wind intensity
markScheme: 1 mark: new predators, new pathogens, availability of food
questions.explanation: All three involve living organisms. The other options each include at least one abiotic factor (light, temperature, moisture, carbon dioxide, pH or wind).

questions.question: In a predator-prey relationship, which animal is the prey?
options: The animal that kills
The animal that is eaten
The animal that causes disease
The plant that is eaten
markScheme: 1 mark: the animal that is eaten
questions.explanation: Prey are animals killed and eaten by predators. A plant eaten by a herbivore is not usually called prey.

questions.question: Grey squirrels obtain nuts more efficiently than red squirrels. Which biotic factor explains the fall in red squirrel numbers?
options: A new pathogen
Lack of light
One species outcompeting another
A new predator arriving
markScheme: 1 mark: one species outcompeting another
questions.explanation: Both species need the same food, and grey squirrels win the competition. Lack of light is abiotic, and grey squirrels do not eat red squirrels, so they are not predators.

questions.question: On a graph of predator and prey numbers, how does the predator curve usually compare with the prey curve?
options: It peaks before the prey curve
It peaks at exactly the same time
It stays constant while the prey curve changes
It peaks after the prey curve and usually at a lower number
markScheme: 1 mark: it peaks after the prey curve and usually at a lower number
questions.explanation: Predators need time to breed after prey increase, so their peak lags behind. There are usually fewer predators than prey because energy is lost at each step in a food chain.

questions.question: Rats were accidentally introduced to an island. The number of ground-nesting seabirds fell sharply. What is the best explanation?
options: The rats competed with the birds for light
The rats were a new predator, and the birds had no defences against them
The rats spread a new abiotic factor
The birds moved away to find more mates
markScheme: 1 mark: the rats were a new predator, and the birds had no defences against them
questions.explanation: Rats eat eggs and chicks. Birds that evolved without ground predators do not hide their nests or defend them, so many are eaten. Animals do not compete for light.

questions.question: A fungus kills most of the ash trees in a wood. Which change is least likely to happen as a direct result?
options: More light reaches the woodland floor
Insects that feed only on ash leaves decline
Soil pH changes because the fungus is abiotic
Other tree species grow into the gaps
markScheme: 1 mark: soil pH changes because the fungus is abiotic
questions.explanation: The fungus is a living pathogen, so it is biotic, not abiotic; the statement is wrong. Losing the ash canopy lets in more light, removes food for ash-feeding insects and opens space for other trees.

questions.question: A predator-prey graph shows that when the predator population is at its highest, the prey population is falling fastest. Which is the best explanation?
options: Prey are dying from a lack of light
The greatest number of predators are eating prey at that time
Predators stop reproducing when there are many of them
Prey breed more slowly when food is abundant
markScheme: 1 mark: the greatest number of predators are eating prey at that time
questions.explanation: Most predators means most prey eaten, so prey decline fastest. Light is abiotic and irrelevant here, and abundant food would increase prey breeding.

questions.question: What usually happens to a population of herbivores when the plants they eat become more plentiful?
options: It decreases
It stays exactly the same
It becomes extinct
It increases
markScheme: 1 mark: it increases
questions.explanation: More food means more herbivores survive and reproduce, so the population increases.

questions.question: Name two biotic factors that can affect a community.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: availability of food; new predators arriving; new pathogens; one species outcompeting another
questions.explanation: These are the four biotic factors in the AQA specification.

questions.question: What does the word biotic mean?
markScheme: 1 mark: living / relating to living organisms
questions.explanation: Biotic factors are caused by living organisms; abiotic means non-living.

questions.question: A new pathogen can spread quickly through a population that has never met it. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the organisms have no resistance / immunity to the new pathogen
1 mark: so most individuals become infected and many die or fail to reproduce
questions.explanation: Without previous exposure there is no resistance in the population, so the pathogen can infect almost every individual.

questions.question: In a wood, owls eat voles. One winter a disease kills most of the voles. Explain what is likely to happen to the owl population.
markScheme: 1 mark: voles are food (prey) for owls, so there is less food
1 mark: more competition between owls for the remaining food
1 mark: fewer owls survive or breed, so the owl population falls
questions.explanation: Food availability is a biotic factor. Losing the prey reduces food, so the predator population falls.

questions.question: Explain why a species of beetle could disappear from an island even though a few individuals are still alive.
markScheme: 1 mark: numbers are too low (for individuals to find mates)
1 mark: so they cannot breed enough to replace those that die
questions.explanation: AQA describes how an outcompeted species may fall to numbers that are no longer sufficient to breed. The population then dies out.

questions.question: Ladybirds were introduced to a greenhouse to control aphids that feed on tomato plants. Explain how this could increase the yield of tomatoes.
markScheme: 1 mark: ladybirds are a new predator that eat aphids, so aphid numbers fall
1 mark: fewer aphids feeding on the plants, so less damage / less sap taken
1 mark: so plants photosynthesise more / have more glucose for growth and fruit production
questions.explanation: This is biological control: deliberately introducing a predator. The chain goes predator up, pest down, crop up.

questions.question: Explain why predator and prey populations in a stable community rise and fall in cycles.
markScheme: 1 mark: when prey increase there is more food so predators increase (after a delay / lag)
1 mark: more predators eat more prey, so prey numbers fall
1 mark: with less food predators then decline, allowing prey to increase again
questions.explanation: Each population controls the other: prey are a food supply for predators, and predators limit prey. This feedback produces repeating cycles.

questions.question: Give one example of a predator and its prey.
markScheme: 1 mark: correctly matched predator and prey, for example fox and rabbit
questions.explanation: Any correctly matched pair where the predator kills and eats the prey is acceptable.

questions.question: A predator-prey graph shows hares rising from 20 000 to 85 000 over two years. Calculate the increase in the number of hares.
questions.explanation: 85 000 − 20 000 = 65 000. Read both values carefully from the axis scale before subtracting.

questions.question: There were 1250 water voles along a stretch of river. After mink escaped from a fur farm, the number fell to 175. Calculate the percentage decrease in water voles.
markScheme: 1 mark: 86%
questions.explanation: 1250 − 175 = 1075. 1075 ÷ 1250 = 0.86. × 100 = 86%. Mink were a new predator that water voles could not escape, as mink swim and can enter their burrows.

questions.question: In a predator-prey cycle, prey numbers peaked in years 3, 13 and 23. Calculate the mean length of one cycle in years.
markScheme: 1 mark: 10 years
questions.explanation: Time between peaks is 10 years each time. (23 − 3) ÷ 2 cycles = 10 years per cycle. Dividing by 3 (the number of peaks) is a common mistake.

questions.question: A wood contained 3200 ash trees. Ash dieback killed 85% of them. A further 40% of the surviving trees then died over the next five years. How many ash trees were left?
markScheme: 1 mark: 3200 × 0.15 = 480 survive the first outbreak
questions.explanation: 15% of 3200 survive: 480. Then 60% of those survive: 480 × 0.6 = 288. Adding the percentages (85% + 40% = 125%) is wrong because the second percentage applies to the survivors only.

questions.question: A cold spring delays the growth of plants in a meadow. Suggest how this could affect a population of caterpillars that feed on the plants.
markScheme: 1 mark: less food available when the caterpillars hatch
1 mark: so fewer survive (to become adults and breed), and the population falls
questions.explanation: The abiotic change (cold) acts through a biotic factor (food availability) on the caterpillars.

questions.question: Foxes eat rabbits and also eat voles. A disease kills most rabbits. Which is the most likely effect on the vole population?
options: Voles increase because foxes have left the area
Voles decrease because foxes eat more voles instead
Voles are unaffected because they do not eat rabbits
Voles increase because they catch the disease
markScheme: 1 mark: voles decrease because foxes eat more voles instead
questions.explanation: With fewer rabbits, foxes switch to their other prey, so more voles are eaten. Voles are affected even though they do not interact with rabbits directly: this is interdependence through a food web.

questions.question: Name the type of organism that kills and eats other animals.
markScheme: 1 mark: predator
questions.explanation: A predator is an animal that kills and eats other animals (its prey).

questions.question: Japanese knotweed is an introduced plant that grows very quickly and forms dense stands up to 3 m tall. Explain how it could affect native plants and animals in a riverbank community.
markScheme: Indicative content: knotweed outcompetes native plants; it shades them, so less light for photosynthesis; takes space, water and mineral ions; native plant numbers fall, may be too few to breed; animals that depend on native plants for food or shelter decline (for example insects, then birds); fewer flowers for pollinators; changes spread through food web.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains competition for named resources leading to loss of native plants, and links this to at least one effect on animals.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that native plants are outcompeted or that animals are affected, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: This is 'one species outcompeting another'. Strong answers follow the effect from plants to the animals that depend on them.

questions.question:
A graph shows the populations of snowshoe hares and lynx in a Canadian forest over 40 years. Both rise and fall in repeating cycles of about 10 years, and the lynx peaks come 1 to 2 years after the hare peaks.
Describe and explain the pattern shown, and suggest one other biotic factor that could also affect the hare population.
markScheme: Indicative content: both populations cycle (rise and fall repeatedly) about every 10 years; lynx peaks lag behind hare peaks by 1 to 2 years; lynx numbers are lower than hare numbers; hares are prey (food) for lynx; when hares increase, more food so more lynx survive and breed; lynx take time to reproduce so there is a lag; more lynx eat more hares so hares fall; with fewer hares, lynx have less food so lynx numbers fall; with fewer predators, hares increase again; other biotic factors: availability of food plants for the hares (plants eaten faster than they regrow); disease or new pathogens spreading when hares are crowded; other predators (owls, foxes); competition with other herbivores.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear description including the lag, full linked explanation of the cycle, and a sensible additional biotic factor with explanation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the pattern and gives some explanation of the link between predator and prey, or gives another biotic factor.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description such as both go up and down, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: A complete answer describes (cycles, lag, relative sizes), explains with a feedback loop between food supply and predation, and adds another biotic factor such as hare food plants or disease.

questions.question: Compare how a new predator and a new pathogen could each reduce the population of a species of wild bird.
markScheme: Indicative content: both are biotic factors; both reduce numbers by killing individuals or reducing breeding; a predator kills and eats birds, eggs or chicks; a pathogen infects birds and causes disease, which may kill them or make them less able to feed or breed; birds may have no defences against a new predator (behaviour) or no resistance to a new pathogen (immunity); pathogens can spread rapidly between birds, especially in crowded colonies; predators are usually limited by how many they can catch; both effects can make the population too small to breed.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): gives at least one similarity and one difference with explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes how one or both reduce numbers without comparing.
questions.explanation: Compare questions need both similarities and differences. Use linking words such as 'both' and 'whereas'.
